text: Square, Inc. is a company headquartered at 1455 Market Street, Suite 600, San Francisco, CA 94103, with a telephone number of (415) 375-3176. The company was incorporated in Delaware and has the IRS Employer Identification Number 80-0429876. It filed an annual report on Form 10-K pursuant to Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2020. Square’s Class A Common Stock trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol SQ. As of June 30, 2020, the aggregate market value of the voting and non-voting common equity held by non-affiliates was approximately $38.7 billion, based on the closing price of the Class A common stock on that date. Shares held by executive officers, directors, and holders of 5% or more of the outstanding Class A or Class B common stock have been excluded from this calculation as such individuals may be deemed affiliates. As of February 18, 2021, the number of outstanding shares of Class A common stock was 389,826,763 and the number of outstanding shares of Class B common stock was 64,787,897. The registrant is a well-known seasoned issuer and has filed all required reports under Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 during the preceding 12 months and has been subject to such filing requirements for the past 90 days. Square has submitted electronically every Interactive Data File required under Rule 405 of Regulation S-T. The company is classified as a large accelerated filer. It has filed a report on and attestation to its management’s assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting under Section 404(b) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. Portions of the registrant’s Definitive Proxy Statement relating to the Annual Meeting of Stockholders are incorporated by reference into Part III of this Form 10-K and will be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission within 120 days after the end of the fiscal year ended December 31, 2020. Square began in February 2009 to enable businesses to accept card payments, and has since expanded to offer over 30 distinct products and services to sellers, including software, hardware, and financial services. The company also operates Cash App, which provides financial services to individuals to help them manage their money. Effective June 30, 2020, Square reported its results under two reportable segments: Seller and Cash App, reflecting the two ecosystems and how management and the chief operating decision maker review business performance. The Seller Ecosystem offers a cohesive commerce platform that helps sellers start, run, and grow their businesses through integrated software, hardware, and financial services, differentiating itself from a fragmented industry that traditionally requires sellers to use multiple vendors and inefficient tools. In the year ended December 31, 2020, Square processed $103.7 billion in Seller Gross Payment Volume (GPV), generated by more than 2 billion card payments from 405 million payment cards, and had over 210 million buyer profiles and approximately 295 million items listed by sellers on its platform. The Cash App Ecosystem provides financial products and services to individuals, including the ability to store, send, receive, spend, and invest money, with the goal of making money more relatable, instantly available, and universally accessible. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, Square made targeted investments in both ecosystems. For sellers, it eliminated fees for software products in March and April 2020, introduced temporary subscription pauses, prioritized omnichannel product launches to support online and contactless commerce, including curbside pickup and delivery, and provided free marketing campaigns to help sellers promote their businesses. As a participant in the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), Square Capital facilitated approximately $857 million in PPP loans, excluding cancelled loans, providing financial support to over 80,000 small businesses as of December 31, 2020. For Cash App customers, the company published educational materials on the CARES Act stimulus programs, expanded direct deposit access to allow customers to receive government funds into their Cash App accounts, and adapted Boost rewards to support pandemic-relevant merchants and categories such as grocery stores. Square’s sellers include a diverse range of businesses across industries such as services, food-related, and retail, and vary in size from sole proprietors to multi-location businesses, spanning the United States, Canada, Japan, Australia, and the United Kingdom. The company serves larger sellers—defined as those generating more than $125,000 in annualized GPV—and GPV from these larger sellers represented 60% of Seller GPV in the fourth quarter of 2020, up from 56% in the fourth quarter of 2019 and 52% in the fourth quarter of 2018. For the years ended December 31, 2020, 2019, and 2018, no single customer accounted for more than 5% of Square’s GPV or total net revenue. The Seller Ecosystem includes software products such as Square Point of Sale, Square Appointments, Square for Retail, and Square for Restaurants, all of which are designed to be self-serve and intuitive, with automatic updates and upgrades. Square Point of Sale is available on iOS and Android and is pre-installed on Square Register and Square Terminal hardware. Square Appointments supports booking, retail sales, invoicing, and payments, includes a free online booking site, and integrates with Square Assistant, an AI-powered messaging tool that helps reduce no-shows. Square for Retail includes barcode scanning, advanced inventory management, support for tens of thousands of items, cost of goods sold reporting, purchase orders, and vendor management. Square for Restaurants includes table, order, and course management, kitchen display systems, and revenue and cost reporting, enabling managers and owners to make informed decisions. All point of sale products have a free tier without a subscription fee, monetized only through transaction fees, while premium tiers of Square Appointments, Square for Retail, and Square for Restaurants are monetized through subscription fees in addition to transaction fees. The company’s online products are part of its broader software suite.

Square Point of Sale is a general-purpose point-of-sale software available on iOS and Android, pre-installed on Square Register and Square Terminal hardware devices. Square Appointments is an integrated solution supporting booking, retail sales, invoicing, and payments, accessible on iOS, Android, and via a web browser, with a free online booking site allowing buyers to schedule appointments, select time, service, and staff. It integrates with Square Assistant, an AI-powered automated messaging tool that responds professionally to buyers, saving seller time and reducing no-shows. Square for Retail is designed for the retail industry, offering barcode scanning, advanced inventory management, support for tens of thousands of items, cost of goods sold reporting, purchase orders, and vendor management. Square for Restaurants is tailored for the food and beverage sector, including table, order, and course management, as well as back-of-house features like a kitchen display system and revenue and cost reporting, enabling managers and owners to make informed decisions. Square’s online products enable sellers to sell via social media and build websites, supporting omnichannel experiences such as buy online, pickup in store (or curbside), and buy online, return in store. All online products offer a free tier without a subscription, monetized solely through transaction fees on payments; premium tiers include additional functionality charged via software fees in addition to transaction fees. Square Online helps sellers across various verticals reach customers through easy website and online store creation, Instagram and Facebook sales, mobile-responsive app-like ordering, QR code ordering for streamlined in-store operations, and fulfillment options including pickup, seller-managed delivery, and partner delivery platforms. Orders, items, inventory, and customer data remain synchronized across online and in-person sales. Square Online Checkout allows sellers to create a checkout link with just a name and price for goods or services without needing a full website. Square Invoices provides a customizable digital invoicing solution with secure online payment acceptance, eliminating the need to print and mail statements or wait for checks; it supports upcoming, recurring, or previously delivered goods and services, such as catering, contractor work, lessons, and retail orders, and allows sending estimates and collecting partial payments. Square Virtual Terminal lets sellers use a computer as a card terminal to take payments, set up recurring billing, record sales, and send digital receipts, including for checks and bank transfers. Business and customer relationship management products streamline operations by integrating with other Square tools, eliminating time-consuming and error-prone data copying and syncing; these are monetized via software fees except for Square Contracts, Feedback, and Dashboard, which are not directly monetized. Square Team Management enables staff scheduling, real-time performance and sales analytics, and employee payments via Square Payroll, with role-based access control; the Square Team App allows team members to clock in/out, view and adjust schedules, see timecards and hours worked, and view estimated pay, and team members paid via Square Payroll can view their pay stubs in the app. Square Contracts helps sellers create custom or template-based digital contracts with e-signature support for service agreements and liability waivers, usable independently or added to Square Invoices or Square Appointments. Square Loyalty, Marketing, Gift Cards, and Feedback help sellers engage customers in-store and online through integrated omnichannel loyalty, marketing, and feedback, with a closed-loop system enabling performance and return on investment assessment. Square Dashboard provides real-time data and insights on orders, items, inventory, customers, employees, payments, marketing, and loyalty performance, accessible via web or the iOS app, enabling timely business decisions. Square offers a developer platform with APIs and SDKs to allow external developers to integrate with its ecosystem. Payment APIs support in-person, online, and mobile payments; the Square Reader SDK enables integration of Square hardware with custom POS systems to build unique checkout experiences like self-ordering kiosks powered by Square’s managed payments; online payments APIs allow integration into e-commerce websites or stores; the In-App Payments SDK enables developers to build consumer mobile apps using Square for payments, primarily monetized through transaction fees. Commerce APIs include over 30 APIs enabling developers to create and manage orders, subscriptions, product catalogs, inventory, customer profiles, employees, loyalty programs, and gift cards, and to build integrations with existing business systems such as accounting, CRM, employee management, and ERP software. Square’s hardware is custom-designed to process all major card types, including magnetic stripe, EMV chip, and NFC, supporting cards from Visa, MasterCard, American Express, Discover, JCB, Interac Flash (in Canada), e-Money (in Japan), and eftpos (in Australia), and can be paired with accessories like cash drawers, receipt printers, and barcode scanners. The hardware portfolio includes a magstripe reader that connects to iOS or Android devices via headphone jack or lightning connector, a contactless and chip reader supporting Apple Pay, Google Pay, and other mobile wallets, the Square Stand that turns an iPad into a payment terminal with integrated magstripe reader, power, and wireless or USB connectivity to a contactless/chip reader, Square Register—an all-in-one device with two screens (seller and customer displays) and a built-in card reader accepting tap, dip, and swipe payments, and Square Terminal, a portable all-in-one payments device and receipt printer with battery lasting all day, accepting tap, dip, and swipe payments. Square acts as both the merchant of record and payment service provider (PSP), managing transaction settlements and risk loss for sellers, leveraging risk assessment models and transaction-level data to onboard new sellers efficiently and inform product development. Square has negotiated direct contracts with acquiring processors and card networks, and indirectly with issuing banks, securing favorable pricing not available to individual sellers. Financial Services include Managed Payments, Business Banking, and Payroll. Managed Payments offers next-day settlements, payment dispute management, data security, and PCI compliance, with onboarding in minutes and transaction fees charged transparently; Risk Manager provides insight into online payment fraud patterns and allows sellers to set custom rules and alerts, using machine learning to identify and adapt to fraud patterns; Instant Transfer enables sellers to receive funds instantly or later the same day, improving cash flow management; Square Card is a free business prepaid debit card that allows sellers to spend proceeds immediately from their Square stored balance, with Square earning interchange fees when purchases are made; Square Capital provides loans to qualified sellers through a partnership with an industrial bank, using a seller’s Square transaction data for underwriting and collections, with loan terms straightforward, repayment automatic via a fixed percentage of card transactions, loans sized under 20% of expected annual GPV, and average repayment in under nine months; since its public launch in May 2014, Square Capital has facilitated over 1.2 million loans and advances totaling more than $8.1 billion, including approximately $857 million in Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loans to over 80,000 sellers in 2020; Square Payroll enables sellers to hire, onboard employees, pay wages and associated taxes, and offer benefits like 401(k) accounts, with competitive differentiation through integration with POS, Team Management, and Cash App. In 2021, Square plans to open an industrial loan corporation, Square Financial Services (SFS), as a wholly owned subsidiary to engage in lending activities related to Square Capital, subject to regulatory approval. Cash App builds an ecosystem to help individuals manage money by making it more accessible, instant, and relatable, primarily serving customers in the U.S. with certain services in Europe (UK and Spain). Customers can store funds via peer-to-peer transfers or bank account deposits, with enhanced onboarding, and use these funds to send money, spend via Cash Card, withdraw at ATMs, invest in stocks or ETFs, buy or sell bitcoin, or transfer to a bank account (instantly for a fee or free in 1–3 days); as of December 31, 2020, Cash App held approximately $2.0 billion in stored balances. Cross-border payments between the U.S. and UK were launched in Q1 2020 with real-time exchange rates and no fees. The Cash Card is a debit card linked directly to a Cash App balance, available for free, usable anywhere that accepts cards, with customers able to select new or promotional designs for a fee; the Cash Boost program offers instant discounts at specific businesses or business types (e.g., 10% off on DoorDash or grocery stores), selected and funded by Square or partners, with Square-funded costs recognized as revenue reductions. Customers can invest in U.S. stocks, ETFs, or bitcoin using funds in their Cash App balance or a linked debit card, with fractional purchases starting at $1, and revenue recognized when bitcoin is purchased and transferred. In Q4 2020, Square acquired Credit Karma Tax, adding a free, mobile-first tax filing product to the Cash App ecosystem. Sales and marketing efforts focus on seller ecosystem growth through brand affinity, direct marketing, public relations, direct sales, and partnerships, with a Net Promoter Score averaging nearly 65 over the past four quarters—double the banking industry average—indicating strong seller recommendations and efficient customer acquisition. Direct marketing channels include search engine optimization, display advertising, direct mail, television ads, mobile advertising, and affiliate and referral programs; direct sales and account management teams support larger sellers, and third-party developers and partners expand reach to sellers with specific needs. Through the Square App Marketplace, partners reach millions of Square users, with over 700 managed partners as of December 31, 2020. Ongoing interactions with sellers through email, in-product notifications, messaging, and Square Communities (an online forum) increase product awareness and usage with minimal incremental sales and marketing costs; customer support also helps increase product usage. Cash App has built a strong brand through compelling features, self-serve experience, unique design, and engaging marketing; peer-to-peer transactions are the primary acquisition channel, with every transfer acquiring or re-engaging a customer, and the service offered for free, considered a marketing tool; peer-to-peer transactions are not revenue-generating, with card issuance, peer-to-peer, and risk loss costs classified as sales and marketing expenses. Paid marketing, including referrals, advertising, partnerships, and social media campaigns, expands the network and improves retention. Launching and advertising new features such as Cash Card, Boost rewards, bitcoin buying and selling, investing in stocks and ETFs, and cross-border payments enhances Cash App’s utility and attracts new users. Both Seller and Cash App products are designed to be cohesive, fast, self-serve, and elegant, with product teams combining product management, engineering, data science, analytics, design, and product marketing; products are platform-agnostic, supporting iOS, Android, and web, and are frequently updated with a rapid software release schedule.

Cash App uses paid marketing strategies, including referrals, advertising, partnerships, and social media campaigns, to grow its network by enhancing its brand, reaching new customers, and improving retention among existing users. The launch and promotion of new features—such as the Cash Card, Boost rewards, bitcoin buying and selling, stock and ETF investing, and cross-border payments—are key methods for attracting new customers, as these features increase the app’s utility and provide compelling reasons for individuals to use it. The company designs both its Seller and Cash App products to be cohesive, fast, self-serve, and elegant, organizing product teams with members from product management, engineering, data science, analytics, design, and product marketing. These products are platform-agnostic, supporting iOS, Android, and web, and are updated frequently with a rapid release schedule. Services are built on a scalable technology platform with a strong emphasis on data analytics and machine learning, enabling the capture and analysis of billions of transactions annually and automating risk assessment for over 99.95% of transactions. Hardware is developed in-house, with production outsourced to third-party manufacturers. In the Seller ecosystem, competitors include manual processes, business software providers (such as point of sale, inventory management, CRM, and invoicing tools), payment terminal vendors, merchant acquirers, banks offering payment processing, loans, and payroll, and alternative lenders. In the Cash App ecosystem, competitors include money transfer apps, prepaid debit card providers, brokerage firms, and crypto trading services. Cash App differentiates itself through its brand, simple and high-quality customer experience, and investments in design and technology. As of December 31, 2020, the company had 5,477 full-time employees worldwide, with 662 outside the U.S., and employs temporary workers and consultants as needed. The company fosters a purpose-driven culture focused on employee input and well-being, offering learning and development programs and a robust manager training program, with employees able to voice feedback through townhall meetings and bi-annual engagement surveys. The shift to remote work began in March 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and in May 2020, the company announced that most employees would continue working remotely even after offices reopened, enabling broader talent sourcing and retention. A key focus in human capital is inclusion and diversity, with 2020 efforts centered on expanding employee resource groups, training managers to lead inclusive teams, and integrating diversity into recruiting. The company publishes annual workforce demographics on its inclusion and diversity blog, with the 2020 report available at https://squareup.com/us/en/l/diversity/representation-matters. From a total rewards perspective, Square offers a competitive compensation and benefits package, reviewed and updated annually, with annual pay equity analyses. Intellectual property is protected through federal, state, and common law rights, contractual agreements with employees and contractors, and via trademarks, trade dress, copyrights, registered domain names, trade secrets, and patents. The company has a patent program to secure patents for innovative products and technologies and actively registers trademarks, logos, service marks, trade dress, and domain names in the U.S. and internationally, including “Square,” “Cash App,” and “Weebly” and their variations. Some intellectual property is licensed from third parties, including under open source licenses, and alternative technologies are available if third-party access is lost. The company is subject to foreign and domestic laws and regulations, and non-compliance could result in license revocation, litigation, investigations, sanctions, or operational constraints. In the U.S., certain jurisdictions require a license to offer peer-to-peer payments, and Cash App holds such licenses and is registered as a “Money Services Business” with the U.S. Department of Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, subject to record-keeping, reporting, bonding, and inspection requirements. Outside the U.S., services are provided through subsidiaries regulated by local authorities, such as an Australian Financial Services License from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission and licenses as an Electronic Money Institution in the U.K. and the European Union. Payments services may face additional regulatory scrutiny, and laws are subject to change and interpretation. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and other agencies regulate financial products and consumer protection, including credit, deposit, and payments services. Cash App is subject to anti-money laundering (AML) laws, with an AML program including policies, procedures, reporting protocols, internal controls, and a designated AML compliance officer to prevent money laundering, terrorist financing, and transactions with sanctioned entities. In 2021, Square obtained a conditional order from the FDIC and the Utah Department of Financial Institutions to open an industrial loan corporation (ILC), which will subject the company to state and federal banking regulations. Cash App Investing LLC operates as a broker-dealer, registered with the SEC and FINRA, and is subject to regulations on marketing, customer asset handling, record-keeping, and reporting, as well as state securities laws. Cash App’s bitcoin services are subject to licensing frameworks, including a New York State Bitlicense, and virtual currency regulations are evolving and subject to change. The company collects and uses customer and third-party data for service integrity and functionality, governed by laws in the U.S., EU, and elsewhere, with privacy policies and terms of service outlining data practices. Communications, including texts and emails, are subject to regulations from the Federal Communications Commission and other bodies. Regulatory agencies continue to examine issues such as products liability, import/export compliance, accessibility, insurance, marketing, privacy, data protection, information security, and labor matters, with additional rules potentially applying if Square expands services like Square Payroll into new jurisdictions. Historically, Seller ecosystem transaction-based revenue peaks in the fourth quarter and is weakest in the first, due to holiday season activity, while subscription and hardware revenue show less seasonality, with fluctuations tied to product launches or promotions. In 2020, Cash App revenue increased significantly, with bitcoin revenue contributing 48% of total consolidated net revenue and 85% of the year’s net revenue growth, driven by customer demand and bitcoin’s market price, which may not reflect future performance and disrupted typical seasonality. Investing in Square involves significant risks, including the ongoing impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, participation in government relief programs, brand protection, customer retention, profitability, product expansion, and the ability to develop products in a rapidly evolving market.

Our business operations face numerous risks and uncertainties, both within and outside our control, which could harm our actual results. Key risks include the ongoing impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and measures taken to contain it, which have negatively affected small businesses—many of which are our sellers—and contributed to reduced economic activity, unemployment, and consumer spending. The pandemic has disrupted operations, including customer support for Cash App, and has led to changes such as remote work, suspended travel, and virtual meetings, with no certainty that these measures are sufficient. The extent of the pandemic’s impact remains highly uncertain and depends on factors like its duration, severity, vaccine availability, and the recovery of economic conditions. Our participation in government relief programs, such as the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) established under the CARES Act in March 2020 and extended until March 31, 2021 with an additional $284 billion allocation, exposes us to new risks. Square Capital, as a PPP participant, provides small businesses with two-year or five-year loans at a 1% fixed interest rate, up to 2.5 times (or 3.5 times for restaurants) their monthly payroll expenses, with loan forgiveness tied to specific spending requirements, including at least 60% for payroll. As of December 31, 2020, Square Capital had facilitated approximately $857 million in PPP loans, excluding cancelled loans, and has retained some loans while selling 100% participation rights to third-party investors; it also borrowed from the Federal Reserve secured by its PPP loan portfolio. These activities expose Square Capital to risks related to documentation, verification, forgiveness, and servicing, including potential losses if borrowers fail to meet requirements or if the SBA declines to honor guarantees. Additionally, Cash App has facilitated economic impact payments and unemployment benefits by providing account and routing numbers and accepting deposits from state-issued prepaid cards, which introduces risks of fraud, data breaches, and technical issues. Our business relies on a strong and trusted brand, and any failure to maintain, protect, or enhance it could harm our operations. Brand strength depends on delivering reliable, secure, and innovative products and services, and on effective marketing, which may be hindered by changes in third-party advertising platforms like Google, Twitter, or Facebook. We also depend on retail partners to sell hardware and acquire customers, and our ability to maintain such partnerships is critical. Harm to our brand can arise from service failures, data misuse, fraud, compliance issues, litigation, or negative publicity. Revenue growth has slowed in the past and may continue to slow, depending on our ability to retain and attract sellers and Cash App customers, as well as to increase sales to both new and existing ones. Our Cash App segment has seen high growth in monthly transacting active customers, but this growth has fluctuated and may decline due to factors like product offerings, network effects, technical issues, fraud, or reputational harm. Government stimulus programs may temporarily boost growth, but such growth may not be sustainable. Cash App revenue growth can be distorted by bitcoin prices, which may not align with customer engagement. We have incurred significant net losses in the past and plan to continue substantial investments in our business, which may prevent us from achieving or maintaining profitability.

A number of factors could negatively impact Cash App customer growth and engagement, including the ability to introduce compelling new products and services, the network effects of other customers’ choices, technical issues affecting the customer experience, insufficient customer support, fraud and scams targeting users, and harm to the company’s reputation and brand. Growth may be temporarily driven by events like government stimulus programs, but such growth may not be sustainable. Cash App revenue growth may be distorted by bitcoin prices, as bitcoin-related revenue fluctuates with market prices and may not align with customer or engagement trends. The company has invested and will continue to invest in improving its Square platform to offer new features, products, and services and to adapt to changing economic conditions; however, if these efforts fail, growth could slow or decline. Despite generating net income of $213.1 million in 2020 and $375.4 million in 2019, the company reported a net loss of $38.5 million in 2018, and as of December 31, 2020, had an accumulated deficit of $297.2 million. The company plans to make significant investments in employee base, sales and marketing, product and service development, acquisitions, infrastructure, international expansion, and general administration, including legal, finance, and compliance costs. If costs for acquiring and supporting new sellers, attracting new Cash App customers, or developing and supporting products and services increase significantly—especially due to third-party advertising fees—expenses could rise sharply. Increases in the seller base may lead to higher losses because upfront costs for new sellers are incurred while revenue is recognized over time. If the company fails to generate sufficient revenue growth and manage expenses, it may incur significant losses and fail to maintain consistent profitability. The company may make decisions that negatively affect short-term operating results if it believes they will improve long-term outcomes, though such decisions may not meet investor expectations or deliver expected long-term benefits, potentially harming the business. Efforts to expand the product portfolio and market reach may not succeed and could reduce revenue growth. While the proportion of revenue from newer products and services has increased in both the Cash App and Seller segments, the company may fail to maintain or grow existing revenue streams or generate significant new ones. New markets may present limited or no prior experience, and the company cannot guarantee that products or services will be widely accepted or that revenue will grow. New technological, operational, regulatory, and other challenges may arise, and service disruptions or failures could materially and adversely affect the business. For example, Cash App products enable investing in assets like bitcoin, stocks, and exchange-traded funds, but users may suffer financial losses due to market fluctuations in these assets. If users are adversely affected, they may stop using the product or Cash App entirely, damaging the brand and reputation. Newer activities may not lead to growth or recoup investments in a timely manner or at all, requiring significant management time and attention, which could harm reputation and limit growth. Long-term success depends on the company’s ability to develop products and services to meet rapidly evolving market demands in payments and financial services; failure to deliver successful enhancements or new features could materially and adversely affect the business. Rapid technological changes, including in omnichannel commerce, proximity payments (e.g., NFC), digital banking, mobile financial apps, and cryptocurrencies and tokenization, may render current products or technologies obsolete or inferior. Incorporating new technologies requires substantial spending and time, and the company may not realize a return on these efforts in a timely manner or at all. Development may be hindered by industry standards, payment card networks, laws and regulations, customer resistance, or third-party intellectual property rights. Success depends on the company’s ability to develop new technologies and adapt to technological changes and evolving standards; failure to keep pace could materially and adversely affect the business. The company relies on third parties, including competitors, for access to new technologies and market development. Failure to anticipate or respond effectively to industry developments may significantly impair operations. Products and services are designed to work with various systems, infrastructures, and devices, requiring continuous modification. Any failure to maintain compatibility with third-party systems could reduce demand, lead to customer dissatisfaction, and materially harm the business. Substantial and increasing competition in the industry may harm the business, as markets are characterized by vigorous competition, changing technology, evolving standards, shifting customer needs, and frequent new product introductions. Competition is expected to intensify as existing and new competitors introduce services or enhance existing ones, including companies not traditionally in the payments space. These competitors may have greater financial resources and larger customer bases, giving them significant advantages, and may devote more resources to product development, promotion, and innovation, achieving economies of scale and outpacing the company’s growth. Mergers and acquisitions by competitors could create even larger, more resource-rich rivals. Some sellers have long-standing exclusive or nearly exclusive relationships with competitors, making it difficult or costly for the company to conduct substantial business with them. Competing services tied to established brands may offer greater perceived safety and effectiveness. If the company cannot differentiate itself, its business will be materially and adversely affected. Pricing pressures may arise as competitors offer lower prices to sellers by cross-subsidizing payments through other services, potentially forcing the company to adjust pricing for sellers and reduce gross profit. Sellers may also demand more customized or favorable pricing, further reducing gross profit. The company currently offers pricing discounts and incentives to large sellers to increase adoption; if a larger proportion of sellers become large sellers, the company may need to increase these discounts, reducing gross profit. Expanding globally presents new challenges and risks, including difficulty attracting sellers or Cash App customers, failing to anticipate local competition, not conforming to business customs, increased costs for protecting intellectual property and sensitive data, changes in business practices, challenges in supporting local third-party providers, difficulties in staffing and managing foreign operations due to cultural, legal, and language differences, challenges in recruiting and retaining employees, difficulties gaining acceptance from industry self-regulatory bodies, compliance with multiple and changing laws (including payments, data privacy, data protection, information security, anti-corruption, anti-bribery, anti-money laundering), potential tariffs, sanctions, fines, trade restrictions, exchange rate risk, complex tax laws, public health issues like the COVID-19 pandemic, and geopolitical instability. These risks could prevent successful global expansion, limiting business growth. Acquisitions, strategic investments, entries into new businesses, joint ventures, divestitures, and other transactions could fail to meet strategic goals, disrupt operations, result in liabilities, harm the business, and negatively impact results. The company regularly evaluates acquisition and investment opportunities, which may divert management attention and incur expenses, even if transactions are not completed. There is no guarantee of success in identifying, negotiating, or completing favorable deals. Risks include failure to advance business strategy, inability to secure regulatory approvals or meet closing conditions, additional regulatory burdens, failure to realize returns or revenue increases, difficulties integrating technologies, IT systems, culture, or personnel, significant acquisition and transition costs, failure to realize expected benefits or synergies, inability to retain key personnel, lack of adequate controls in acquired businesses, undetected liabilities, failure to enter new markets or geographies, inability to retain customers, vendors, or partners, lawsuits or regulatory actions, undetected security weaknesses, local and foreign regulations, and potential dilutive equity issuances or debt incurrence. Divestitures may face difficulties in securing acceptable terms, may involve loss of revenue or margin erosion, or fail to achieve desired strategic or financial benefits. For example, in 2019, the company sold Caviar to DoorDash for cash and stock; following DoorDash’s IPO, the company is required to mark its equity holdings to market quarterly, which may cause fluctuations in results due to DoorDash stock price. The lock-up agreement restricts the company from selling all equity holdings for 180 days post-IPO, and there is no assurance of fully realizing the stock value upon sale. Such transactions may delay strategic objectives, incur additional expenses, disrupt relationships, and expose the company to unanticipated liabilities, including indemnification obligations. During a divestiture, risks include business decline, loss of employees or customers, supplier issues, or failure to close, all of which could materially harm the divested business. If a divestiture is not completed, the company may not find a buyer on the same terms and may have incurred significant costs without benefit. Joint ventures and minority investments involve reduced control, increasing financial, legal, operational, regulatory, and compliance risks. The company may be dependent on joint venture partners, controlling shareholders, or management with conflicting interests, whose decisions or actions could harm the investment, lead to litigation or regulatory action, or damage the company’s reputation and brand. Square Capital faces additional risks related to capital availability, seller payments, bank partnership structure, product expansion, regulatory obligations, and macroeconomic conditions. Its growth depends on institutional third-party investors purchasing business loans originated by the bank partner. If these investors reduce purchases or stop buying loans, the bank partner may reduce originations, or the company may need to fund loan purchases from its own resources, potentially forcing a reduction in Square Capital’s scale. Square Capital has repurchase obligations in loan purchase and servicing agreements for breaches of eligibility representations or warranties. Revenue is recognized when control of the promised goods or services is transferred to customers, in an amount that reflects the consideration the Company expects to be entitled to in exchange for those goods or services. Transaction-based revenue: The Company charges its sellers a transaction fee for managed payments solutions that is generally calculated as a percentage of the total transaction amount processed. The Company collects the transaction amount from the seller's customer's bank, net of acquiring interchange and assessment fees, processing fees, and bank settlement fees paid to third-party payment processors and financial institutions. The Company retains its fees and remits the net amount to the sellers. The Company acts as the merchant of record for its sellers and works directly with payment card networks and banks so that its sellers do not need to manage the complex systems, rules, and requirements of the payments industry. The Company satisfies its performance obligations and therefore recognizes the transaction fees as revenue upon authorization of a transaction by the seller's customer's bank. The Company applies the optional exemption allowed under ASC 606 not to disclose consideration attributable to performance obligations for future transaction processing since the term of the contract with a seller is not defined and any future consideration on the contract would be dependent on the value and volume of transactions processed in the future, which are not determinable. Revenue is recognized net of refunds, which arise from reversals of transactions initiated by sellers. The transaction fees collected from sellers are recognized as revenue on a gross basis as the Company is the principal in the delivery of the managed payments solutions to the sellers. The Company has concluded it is the principal because as the merchant of record, it controls the services before delivery to the seller, it is primarily responsible for the delivery of the services to its sellers, and it has discretion in setting prices charged to sellers. The Company also has the unilateral ability to accept or reject a transaction based on criteria established by the Company. As the merchant of record, Square is liable for the costs of processing the transactions for its sellers, and records such costs within cost of revenue. Subscription and services-based revenue: Subscription and services-based revenue is primarily comprised of revenue the Company generates from Instant Deposit and Cash Card, Square Capital, website hosting and domain name registration services, and various other software as a service (SaaS) products. Instant Deposit is a functionality within the Cash App and the Company's managed payments solution that enables customers, including individuals and sellers, to instantly deposit funds into their bank accounts. The Company charges a per transaction fee which is recognized as revenue when customers instantly deposit funds to their bank account. The Company also offers Cash App customers the ability to use funds stored in the Cash App via a Visa prepaid card (Cash Card), for which the Company charges a per transaction fee that is recorded as revenue. Square Capital facilitates a loan that is offered through a partnership with an industrial bank that is either repaid through withholding a percentage of the collections of the seller's receivables processed by the Company or a specified monthly amount. The Company generally facilitates loans to its sellers through a pre-qualification process that includes an analysis of the aggregated data of the seller’s business which includes, but is not limited to, the seller’s historical processing volumes, transaction count, chargebacks, growth, and length of time as a Square customer. The Company also facilitates loans to the customers of certain sellers as well as to the sellers of its partners who do not process payments through the Company. The loans are generally originated by a bank partner, from whom the Company purchases the loans obtaining all rights, title, and interest. The loans have no stated coupon rate but the seller is charged a one-time origination fee by the bank partner based upon their risk rating, which is derived primarily from processing activity. It is the Company’s intent to sell all of its rights, title, and interest of these loans to third-party investors for an upfront fee when the loans are sold. The Company records the net amounts paid to the bank as the cost of the loans purchased and subsequently records a gain on sale of the loans to the third-party investors as revenue upon transfer of title. The Company is retained by the third-party investors to service the loans and earns a servicing fee for facilitating the repayment of these receivables through its managed payments solutions. The Company records servicing revenue as servicing is delivered. For the loans which are not immediately sold to third-party investors, the Company recognizes a portion of the expected seller repayments over the cost of the loans as revenue in proportion to the loan principal reduction. The Company also acts as a reseller of domain names registration services for a registrar for a fee, which is also generally billed at inception. The Company considers that it satisfies its performance obligations over time and as such recognizes revenue ratably over the term of the relevant arrangements, which vary from one month to twenty four months for website hosting, and one year to ten years for domain name registration. SaaS represents software products and solutions that provide customers with access to various technologies for a fee which is recognized as revenue ratably as the service is provided. Hardware revenue: The Company generates revenue through the sale of hardware through e-commerce and through its retail distribution channels. The Company satisfies its performance obligation upon delivery of hardware to its customers who include end user customers, distributors, and retailers. The Company allows for customer returns which are accounted for as variable consideration. The Company estimates these amounts based on historical experience and reduces revenue recognized. The Company invoices end user customers upon delivery of the products to customers, and payments from such customers are due upon invoicing. Distributors and retailers have payment terms that range from 30 to 90 days after delivery. The Company offers hardware installment sales to customers with terms ranging from three to twenty four months. The Company allocates a portion of the consideration received from these arrangements to a financing component when it determines that a significant financing component exists. The financing component is subsequently recognized as financing revenue separate from hardware revenue, within subscription and services-based revenue, over the terms of the arrangement with the customer. Pursuant to practical expedients afforded under ASC 606, the Company does not recognize a financing component for hardware installment sales that have a term of one year or less. Bitcoin revenue: The Company offers its Cash App customers the ability to purchase bitcoin, a cryptocurrency denominated asset, from the Company. The Company satisfies its performance obligation and records revenue when bitcoin is transferred to the customer's account. The Company purchases bitcoin from private broker dealers or from Cash App customers and applies a small margin before selling it to its customers. The sale amounts received from customers are recorded as revenue on a gross basis and the associated bitcoin cost as cost of revenues, as the Company is the principal in the bitcoin sale transaction. The Company has concluded it is the principal because it controls the bitcoin before delivery to the customers, it is primarily responsible for the delivery of the bitcoin to the customers, it is exposed to risks arising from fluctuations of the market price of bitcoin before delivery to customers, and has discretion in setting prices charged to customers. Operating lease right-of-use assets and operating lease liabilities are recognized at the present value of future lease payments, generally for the base noncancellable lease term, at the lease commencement date. The interest rate used is the Company's incremental borrowing rate, as the interest rate implicit in most leases is not readily determinable. The incremental borrowing rate approximates the rate the Company would pay to borrow on a collateralized basis with similar terms and payments as the lease, in the economic environment where the leased asset is located. Operating lease right-of-use assets include prepaid lease payments and lease incentives. Lease agreements generally contain lease and non-lease components; non-lease components, such as maintenance and utilities, are combined with lease payments and accounted for as a single lease component. Fixed non-lease components are included in the determination of right-of-use assets and operating lease liabilities. The Company records amortization of the right-of-use asset and accretion of the lease liability as a component of rent expense in the consolidated statement of operations. Accounting for finance leases remained substantially unchanged.
